misconceptions.description: Building the classroom routine around what a new device or app can do rather than around the learning move the routine should support
misconceptions.trigger: teacher justifies a routine by listing tool features such as timers, dashboards, or polls instead of the instructional purpose those features serve
misconceptions.feedback: State the learning move first, then ask whether the tool affordance actually serves it. A routine that exists to use the tool, not to teach, is the warning sign.

misconceptions.description: Reading high student engagement with a tech routine as proof that learning is happening
misconceptions.trigger: teacher cites that students were on task or excited as the justification for keeping the routine
misconceptions.feedback: Engagement is necessary but not sufficient. Point to a learning artifact or check the routine produced, not just attention.

misconceptions.description: Assuming every student can run the routine identically because the school provides devices, ignoring connectivity, accommodations, and home constraints
misconceptions.trigger: routine has no fallback for a student whose device, login, or bandwidth fails
misconceptions.feedback: Map who is excluded when the tech fails. A defensible routine names the non-digital fallback that keeps the learning move intact.
